title: Integer Arithmetic & Overflow
summary: Addition and subtraction run through the same adder circuit for signed and unsigned numbers — but the two flavors disagree on what counts as overflow, and getting that wrong is a real source of bugs.

slides.subTitle: Bit by bit, with carry
slides.markdown:
Binary addition works exactly like the long addition you learned in school, just with only two digits. Add each bit position with any incoming carry, and if the result exceeds 1, a carry ripples to the next position:

```
  0111  (7)
+ 0011  (3)
------
  1010  (10)
```

The hardware circuit that does this — a chain of 1-bit adders passing a carry forward — is **identical whether the operands are signed or unsigned**. The bits don't know or care what encoding they represent; that meaning is only assigned when you *interpret* the result.

slides.subTitle: Subtraction is just addition
slides.markdown:
Because two's complement made addition uniform, subtraction gets a free ride: `a - b` is computed as `a + (-b)`, where `-b` is b's two's-complement negation (invert, add 1).

That means hardware needs **no separate subtractor circuit** — an adder plus a bit-inverter on one input (fed a control signal for +1) handles both operations. This is a direct payoff of the two's-complement choice from the previous topic: one circuit, two operations.

slides.subTitle: The carry-in vs carry-out rule
slides.markdown:
**Signed overflow** happens exactly when the carry **into** the sign bit differs from the carry **out of** the sign bit. If they match, the sign bit settled correctly; if they differ, the result's sign bit is a lie.

Example in 4 bits: `0111 (7) + 0001 (1)`. Carry into bit 3 (the sign bit) is 1; carry out of bit 3 is 0 — they differ, so this is signed overflow (the true answer, 8, doesn't fit in 4-bit signed range and wraps to `1000` = -8). This single XOR of two carry bits is exactly how hardware computes the overflow flag.

slides.subTitle: A ripple-carry adder's outputs
slides.markdown:
A ripple-carry adder chains 1-bit full adders, each passing its carry to the next, and exposes both a final carry-out and (from the top two carries) an overflow signal:

![A ripple-carry adder chain producing a sum, a carry-out, and an overflow flag](assets/ripple-carry-adder.svg)

Each full adder takes two operand bits plus carry-in, and produces a sum bit plus carry-out. The overflow flag taps the carry into and out of the *last* (sign-bit) adder specifically — every other stage's carry is irrelevant to signed overflow.

assets.alt: A ripple-carry adder chain producing a sum, a carry-out, and an overflow flag

slides.subTitle: Carry flag vs overflow flag
slides.markdown:
The *same* addition produces two independent flags with different meanings:

- **Carry flag (unsigned overflow)** — set when the final carry-out (past the top bit) is 1: the **unsigned** result didn't fit.
- **Overflow flag (signed overflow)** — set when carry-in and carry-out of the sign bit differ: the **signed** result didn't fit.

The same bit pattern can trip one flag, both, or neither depending on whether you *meant* the operands as signed or unsigned — hardware computes both every time and lets the instruction decide which matters.

slides.subTitle: A real wraparound bug
Wraparound vs saturating arithmetic
slides.markdown:
General-purpose CPUs default to **wraparound** (modular) arithmetic — overflow silently wraps, as seen above. Some domains instead want **saturating** arithmetic — overflow clamps to the min/max representable value instead of wrapping.

| | Wraparound | Saturating |
|---|---|---|
| Default in | General-purpose ISAs (x86, ARM integer ops) | Audio/DSP/SIMD instructions (`vqadd`, `paddsb`) |
| Overflow behavior | Wraps to the opposite extreme | Clamps at max/min |
| Why | Cheapest, most predictable for general code | Wrapping in audio would sound like a loud pop/glitch |

Use saturating arithmetic where a wrapped value would be actively harmful (audio samples, pixel blending) rather than just numerically wrong.

slides.subTitle: Signed overflow is undefined behavior
slides.markdown:
Unlike unsigned overflow (well-defined wraparound in C/C++), **signed integer overflow is undefined behavior** in C and C++ — the standard doesn't require wraparound, a trap, or any specific result.

This isn't just theoretical: optimizing compilers actively **assume signed overflow never happens** and can eliminate checks like `if (x + 1 < x)` entirely, because that condition is 'impossible' under the standard's assumptions — silently removing an overflow check you wrote on purpose. Use `INT_MAX` bounds checks *before* the addition, or unsigned/wrapping-safe types, never after.
